prompt: A new restaurant gets two 5-star reviews and claims it's the best in town.
why: Two reviews could easily be the owner's friends or luck. With so few data points, the result can't support the claim.
trap: Not who reviewed, but how few.

prompt: A coin lands heads 4 times out of 5, and someone calls it unfair.
why: A fair coin gives 4 heads out of 5 quite often by chance. Five flips are too few to judge whether it's fair.
trap: There's no bias in who was asked.

prompt: A small hospital has the most extreme share of baby boys in some years, high and low, just by chance.
why: With few births, the share of boys swings widely by chance from year to year. Small samples produce the most extreme results, high and low.
trap: Nothing is wrong with which births are counted.

prompt: A drug test with 6 patients shows a big effect that disappears in a trial of 600.
why: With only 6 patients, chance can create a big effect that vanishes with 600. Small samples swing; large ones settle near the truth.
trap: The larger trial is the same kind of patients.

prompt: A survey of 10 people says 70% love the product.
why: With 10 people, 7 saying yes could easily be chance. The sample is too small to trust the 70%.
trap: Nothing says who the ten were.

prompt: The more games a player plays, the closer their win rate settles to their true skill.
why: Early on, a few lucky or unlucky games move the win rate a lot. With more games it settles near true skill: the law of large numbers.
trap: It isn't a link between two measures.
